description: Toy Box Friends G5-05: energy in ecosystems. Producers make food from sunlight, consumers eat, decomposers recycle matter, arrows point the way energy flows, and about a tenth passes up each step of the energy pyramid. No animal ever catches another on screen: energy dots do the moving.

meta.title: Ecosystem Energy: food chains and webs

youtube.title: Food Chains and Food Webs for Kids | Producers and Consumers | Grade 5 Science | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Where does a banana's energy come from? Monkey says the soil, but glowing energy dots show it really started in the Sun! Robo, Monkey and Bear follow the energy through a forest.
You'll learn: producers make food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (photosynthesis); herbivores, carnivores and omnivores; food chain arrows point from the eaten to the eater, the way energy flows; decomposers recycle matter into the soil; food webs and what happens when one part disappears; and why only about a tenth of the energy passes up each step.
Try at home: trace your lunch back to the Sun with arrows. Outdoors with a grown-up, look for decomposers under a log, but never touch or eat wild mushrooms, and wash your hands after.

objects.text: sunlight + water + carbon dioxide → sugar (food) + oxygen
The arrow means "gives energy to". It points from the eaten to the eater.
Decomposers break down dead leaves and living things into nutrients in the soil.
Matter goes round and round. Energy does not: plants need new sunlight every day.
Fun fact: earthworms have no lungs. They breathe through their skin!
Frogs lose food. Hawks may eat more mice. Grass may grow taller.
About one tenth of the energy passes up each step. The rest is used to live and grow, or lost as heat.
Fun fact: plants catch only a small part of the sunlight, yet it feeds almost every food chain on land.
1. Where does almost all the energy in a food chain come from?
2. In Sun → grass → bunny → fox, which way do the arrows point?
From the eaten to the eater: the way energy flows.
3. Is a bear a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore?
4. Why are there fewer foxes than bunnies?
Only about a tenth of the energy passes up each step.

do.text: Ecosystem Energy: food chains and webs
Mmm, a banana! Where does a banana's energy come from?
The banana plant! And the plant got it from... the soil?
Let's follow the energy. Watch the golden dot.
From the Sun, to the leaf, to the banana, to you. Your jump started in the Sun!
Today: how energy flows through an ecosystem.
ecosystem
Green plants are producers. They make their own food. Here's how.
producer
Sunlight shines on the leaves.
Water comes up from the roots.
Carbon dioxide comes in from the air.
The leaf turns them into sugar, its food, and gives off oxygen.
Quick check: what three things does a leaf need to make its food?
Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide!
This is called photosynthesis.
So plants eat soil, right? That's why they grow in it!
Not quite. Soil gives water and nutrients, but plants make their own food from sunlight.
Plants are food factories! Powered by the Sun.
In our forest, the producers are grass, oak trees with acorns, and berry bushes.
Animals can't make their own food. They are consumers: they eat to get energy.
consumer
Herbivores eat only plants. The bunny and the grasshopper eat grass.
herbivore
The squirrel eats mostly acorns and seeds. Herbivore too!
Carnivores eat other animals. The frog eats insects.
carnivore
Is the hawk a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore?
Carnivore! Hawks eat mice, frogs and bunnies.
Omnivores eat plants and animals. The mouse eats seeds and insects.
omnivore
The fox eats bunnies, mice and berries. Which group is the fox in?
Plants and animals: omnivore! And me too. I eat fruit, leaves and insects.
And I eat berries, acorns and insects. I'm an omnivore too!

scenes.title: A food chain and the arrow rule

do.text: A food chain shows who eats what. Sun, grass, bunny, fox.
Let me draw the arrows! The fox points at what it eats.
Let's send the energy along your arrows.
The energy can't get from the Sun to the fox. The arrows point the wrong way!
Which way should the arrows point?
The arrow means gives energy to. It points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats.
Now the dots flow all the way! Sun to grass to bunny to fox.
The grass is the producer. The bunny is the first consumer, and the fox is the second consumer.
So every food chain starts with the Sun, then a producer.
Here's another chain: Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, hawk.
Producer, first consumer, second consumer, third consumer.
What happens when leaves fall and living things die? Meet the decomposers.
decomposer
Mushrooms and other fungi, tiny bacteria, and helpers like worms break them down.
They turn them into nutrients in the soil.
Then plants take the nutrients up through their roots.
So decomposers are nature's recyclers!
Yes! Matter goes round and round. But energy does not.
Energy is used up or lost as heat, so plants need new sunlight every day.

do.words: plants need new sunlight every day

do.text: If you went looking for decomposers, where would you find the most?
In damp, shady places, like under logs and leaves!
Fun fact: earthworms have no lungs. They breathe through their skin.
And one honey fungus in Oregon spreads underground for about nine square kilometers!
In a real forest, food chains join together. This is a food web.
food web
Grass feeds the bunny, the grasshopper and the mouse.
Acorns feed the squirrel, the mouse and the bear.
Berries feed the bear and the fox. The frog eats grasshoppers.
The fox eats bunnies and mice. The hawk eats mice, squirrels, frogs and bunnies.
And the bear eats insects too.
Look! I'm in lots of chains: berries, acorns and insects all give me energy.
One animal can be in many food chains. Now, a prediction.
What if all the grasshoppers disappeared? What would happen?
The frog loses its food! There might be fewer frogs.
And the hawk may hunt more mice instead. The grass may grow taller, with nobody nibbling it.
Changing one part of a web can change many others.
Why are there lots of plants, fewer bunnies and only a few foxes? Let's count energy.
Say one thousand units of energy go into the grass.
The grass uses most of it to live and grow, and some is lost as heat.
Only about one hundred units pass up to the bunnies.
And only about ten reach the foxes.
About one tenth passes up at each step. It's a rough rule.
Check: if a field of clover had two thousand units, about how many would reach the next step?
About one tenth: two hundred!
That's why there's more grass than bunnies, and more bunnies than foxes!
Fun fact: plants catch only a small part of the sunlight.
But it feeds almost every food chain on land!
Where does the energy start?
The Sun!
Which way do arrows go?
To the eater!
Sun to the leaf and leaf to me! Follow the arrow, follow the energy!
Clap and pass it! Sun to the leaf and leaf to me! Follow the arrow, follow the energy!
Detective challenge! This web has three mistakes. Can you find them?
find 3 mistakes
Mistake one: look at the arrow between the hawk and the mouse.
It's backwards! The mouse gives energy to the hawk.
Mistake two: something is missing that every web needs.
The Sun! Producers need sunlight.
Mistake three: this mushroom is labelled producer.
A mushroom can't make food from sunlight. It's a decomposer!
Three mistakes fixed. Great detective work!
Question one. Where does almost all the energy in a food chain come from?
The Sun!
Question two. In Sun, grass, bunny, fox, which way do the arrows point, and why?
From the eaten to the eater, the way the energy flows.
Question three. Is a bear a herbivore, a carnivore or an omnivore?
An omnivore. Bears eat plants and animals.
Question four. Why are there fewer foxes than bunnies?
Only about a tenth of the energy passes up at each step.
Recap! Producers make food from sunlight. Consumers eat. Decomposers recycle matter.
Arrows follow the energy, and there's less energy at each step.
Everyone in the forest is connected!
Your turn! Pick a food from your lunch and trace it back to the Sun with arrows.
Sun → wheat → bread → you
Outdoors, look for decomposers under a log. Look, but don't touch or eat wild mushrooms.
Go with a grown-up and wash your hands after. See you next time!
